options: Triggering a build and automated test run on every commit, without a human manually starting it
Automatically writing the release notes for every deploy
Approving every release without human sign-off
Choosing which features to build next sprint
questions.explain: CI means every commit automatically triggers a build and test run, catching problems before a human has to find them by hand.

questions.q: What's the difference between Continuous Delivery and full Continuous Deployment?
options: Continuous Delivery packages a change and makes it ready to release; full Continuous Deployment automatically promotes it all the way to Production
They are exactly the same thing with different names
Continuous Delivery only applies to database changes
Continuous Deployment means no automated tests are run
questions.explain: Continuous Delivery means a change that passes CI is packaged and ready to go; a full Continuous Deployment setup goes further and automatically promotes it through to Production.

questions.q: Which item is NOT part of the release checklist described in this lesson?
options: Rewriting the entire codebase before each release
Approval from someone with authority
Monitoring immediately after the change lands
A tested rollback plan
questions.explain: The real release checklist covers approval, monitoring, a rollback plan, and release notes — rewriting the codebase before each release isn't part of it.

questions.q: What makes a Canary deployment lower-risk than releasing to 100% of users at once?
options: The new version ships to a small slice of real users first, and the rollout only widens once that slice looks healthy
Canary deployments skip automated testing entirely
Canary deployments only work for database changes
Canary deployments require no monitoring
questions.explain: A Canary deployment sends the new version to a small slice of users first — if that slice looks healthy, the rollout widens; if not, the blast radius of a bad release stays small.

questions.q: What does a feature flag let a team do that a normal deployment alone doesn't?
options: Ship code to Production switched off, then turn it on independently of the deployment itself
Skip the Dev environment entirely
Avoid writing any automated tests
Deploy directly from a developer's laptop with no pipeline
questions.explain: A feature flag lets code ship 'dark' — present in Production but switched off — and be enabled later, independently of deployment. That's how a team can deploy on one day and launch on a different day without a second deploy.
